title: Covariance estimation from MCMC chains
one_liner: When you sample from a hard distribution using a Markov chain, the measurements can estimate covariance as well as random independent samples, but with far fewer queries to the distribution.
lead: Measuring spread and correlation is one of the most basic statistical tasks. Normally you grab many independent random samples and compute the spread yourself. But for hard problems—like estimating how particles move in a confined space—you can only sample by running a long slow chain (Markov chain Monte Carlo). This paper asks: can those slow chain samples measure spread and correlation as well as independent samples? The answer is yes, and you might need fewer queries.

paras: To describe a cloud of scattered data, you need two numbers: how spread out it is (variance) and how the spread correlates across dimensions (covariance matrix). The standard way: grab many independent samples and calculate. But some problems forbid independence. Imagine sampling from the shape of a confined space. The only way to explore it is to walk randomly from point to point—each new point is correlated with the last, not independent. This is a Markov chain: each step depends on where you just were.

A naive thought: use the correlated samples anyway, just like independent ones. This breaks because the measurements are biased—you see phantom spread and phantom correlations that come from the chain's memory, not from the actual shape you are trying to learn.

callout.html: If the chain mixes well (stops depending on where it started) and the shape of the data is smooth enough, dependent chain samples can estimate covariance as accurately as independent ones.

panels.title: 1. The data lives in a valley
panels.caption: A distribution is a valley; you need to know its shape.

panels.title: 2. Random walk explores it
panels.caption: Each step of the chain sits in the valley, but each depends on the last.

panels.title: 3. Naive measurement fails
panels.caption: Treating dependent steps as independent corrupts the spread measurement.

panels.title: 5. Better than you need
panels.caption: You reach the same accuracy with fewer calls to the distribution.

steps.text: You have a long walk through the distribution, each point correlated with the previous one.
Check that the chain stops depending on its starting point (mixes) and that the distribution is smooth locally.
Apply a bias-corrected formula that accounts for how much the chain's steps overlap in memory.
Show that the error shrinks at the same rate—with enough chain steps you get the same precision.
The key win: you used fewer calls to the distribution than independent sampling would require.

paras: The paper does not change the distribution or the chain algorithm. It changes the estimator—the formula you apply to a chain's output to measure covariance. Instead of naively averaging products of deviations (which is biased when samples are correlated), it uses a weighted average that cancels out the chain's memory.

hidden.h2: The mixing time: how fast the chain forgets
hidden.name: spectral gap
paras: The paper measures a hidden property of the Markov chain: how fast it forgets where it started. This is called the spectral gap—a number between 0 and 1. If the gap is large, the chain loses memory quickly (good for independent estimates). If the gap is tiny, the chain remembers a long time (samples are highly correlated).

The paper bounds this gap using another mathematical property called a Poincaré inequality—a guarantee that the distribution is smooth locally, not lumpy or disconnected. From these two properties, the paper derives how many chain steps you actually need to collect.

heat.caption: Darker means the chain's memory is stronger at that lag; highlight shows which lags matter most for the bias correction.

reads.html: The spectral gap is the speed at which random memory leaks out of the chain. Bigger gap means shorter memory and more independent-like behavior.
Under Poincaré inequality, the spectral gap lower-bounds the rate at which the chain's dependence on its initial state decays exponentially.

paras: A dependent sample carries correlation with the samples around it. When you compute covariance naively—averaging products of deviations—you double-count the effect of each correlation, because every pair of nearby samples reinforces the signal. The paper's key insight: weight each lag (time distance between samples) by how much correlation it actually contributes. Far-away samples are nearly independent, so their weight is small. Recent samples are highly correlated, but you can measure exactly how much from the chain's transition probabilities.

The Poincaré inequality says: if the shape is smooth everywhere, the chain mixes uniformly. This means you can derive a universal bound—no matter which dimension you are measuring, the same number of samples suffices to cancel the bias. With that guarantee, you can build a covariance estimator that works for any Gibbs distribution (a huge class including neural networks, physics simulations, and constrained optimization).

stages.s: Weight lags by how much they overlap
Subtract weighted bias from sample covariance

math.words: bias-corrected covariance = sample covariance minus weighted sum of autocorrelation terms at each lag, where weights decay by the spectral gap
symbols: the spectral gap (how fast chain forgets; between 0 and 1)
the time lag (distance between samples in the chain)
the autocorrelation at lag k (how much a sample correlates with itself k steps later)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a one-dimensional sample has raw covariance 10.0, spectral gap rho = 0.9 (chain forgets slowly).
Lag 1 autocorrelation C_1 = 2.0; lag 2 autocorrelation C_2 = 0.5; higher lags negligible.
Corrected covariance: 10.0 - 3.896 = 6.104. This is closer to the truth than the raw 10.0.

math.note: The weight rho^(2k) decays exponentially with lag—nearby samples' memory is subtracted heavily, distant samples barely matter.

charts.title: Naive (biased) estimator
charts.note: Bias does not shrink even with more samples; dependent structure corrupts every estimate.

charts.title: Corrected estimator
charts.note: After accounting for chain memory, error shrinks at the correct rate and vanishes with enough samples.

items.b: If the distribution has disconnected regions.
items.html: The chain will get stuck in one region and never visit others. The Poincaré inequality fails, and the corrected formula breaks. The fix: verify that the distribution is connected and smoothly mixed.

items.b: If you start with a bad initialization.
items.html: Early chain samples reflect the starting point, not the true distribution. You need a burn-in period. The paper's bounds account for this but require discarding the first many steps.

items.b: If the spectral gap is tiny.
items.html: The chain forgets very slowly, so samples remain highly dependent. You need exponentially more samples to cancel the bias. The fix: use a faster-mixing chain algorithm or better initialization, because a larger spectral gap means samples decorrelate faster, reducing the bias term and cutting the number of samples you need.

items.b: Done right: start after burn-in, verify smooth distribution, collect enough samples relative to the spectral gap.
items.html: Then the corrected estimator provably recovers the true covariance with high probability, using far fewer queries than independent sampling.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate a simple Gibbs distribution (e.g., a 2D Gaussian or a Gaussian truncated to a simplex). Run a random walk chain (Metropolis or Langevin dynamics). Collect samples after burn-in. Compute the spectral gap numerically (trace a few power-iteration steps or use known formulas for the test distribution). Apply both the naive covariance and the corrected formula. Measure error as the Frobenius norm (the length of the difference matrix). Plot: error versus chain length for both estimators. Show that the corrected error decays with the same rate as independent sampling, while naive stays biased.
demo.metric_eq: error = ||Sigma_estimated - Sigma_true||_F (Frobenius norm: square root of sum of squared differences)
demo.closing: The corrected estimator should converge to zero error; the naive estimator should plateau at a nonzero bias. Switching to the corrected formula is a free win for any MCMC application.
